title: Employee Retention Strategies
subject: Human Resources
description: Understand why people leave, use stay and exit interviews well, build visible career paths, and recognise good work in ways that matter.

lessons.title: Why people leave
lessons.body:
People usually leave for a combination of reasons. Common ones include:

- **Manager relationship:** the strongest single driver of whether people stay.
- **Career growth:** no visible next step or chance to learn.
- **Pay and benefits:** important, but rarely the only reason.
- **Workload and burnout:** sustained overwork.
- **Purpose and recognition:** not seeing how the work matters, or not being thanked for it.

Look at attrition by team, manager, tenure, and role. Patterns usually point to a specific fixable cause.

lessons.title: Stay interviews and exit interviews
lessons.body:
A stay interview is a conversation with a current employee, held before any resignation, to learn what keeps them and what could make them leave. Useful questions include: 'What keeps you here?' 'What would make you consider leaving?' 'What would you change about your role if you could?'

An exit interview is held when someone resigns. It is most useful when the person is candid, so hold it with someone outside their reporting line, and let them know their answers will be used to improve things, not to judge them. Record the reasons in a consistent format so patterns can be analysed.

lessons.title: Career paths and development
lessons.body:
Employees stay when they can see where their career could go. A career path shows the roles a person can move to, the skills each role needs, and the steps to get there.

Practical steps:

- Agree on a development plan with each employee at least once a year.
- Offer stretch assignments, mentoring, and access to learning.
- Make internal moves visible, and prefer internal candidates for open roles where they are ready.

Development conversations are more useful when they are regular and specific, not only at review time.

lessons.title: Recognition that works
lessons.body:
Recognition is most effective when it is specific, timely, and linked to behaviour. 'Thank you for the handover notes, they saved the team a day' means more than a general 'good job'.

Avoid assuming that one reward suits everyone. Some people value public thanks, others value time off, learning, or a conversation with senior leaders. Ask what each person values, and check whether recognition is applied fairly across teams.
